title: What will be the total spending by all Senate candidates in the 2026 US election cycle?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve to the total spending by all US Senate candidates running in 2026 according to the [Federal Election Commission](https://www.fec.gov/data/spending-bythenumbers/) (FEC).
fine_print: This question may wait until December 31, 2026, to ensure that all data is updated and included.
background:
The 2026 midterm elections are scheduled to be held on November 3, 2026. The US Senate has 100 seat seats. [As of early 2025](https://ballotpedia.org/119th_United_States_Congress), 53 are held by members of the Republican Party, 45 are held by Democrats, and 2 are held by independents who [caucus with](https://www.senate.gov/about/glossary.htm#C) the Democrats.

Senators are elected for 6-year terms, and elections are held every two years, such that in each election approximately 1/3 of the seats are up for contest. For 2026, [the 33 seats of "Class II" are scheduled for election](https://www.senate.gov/senators/Class_II.htm). As of early 2025, 20 are held by Republicans and 13 of those seats are held by Democrats. The 33 winners of the 2026 Senate elections will join 66 incumbent Senators and the winners of the concurrent House elections to form the 120th Congress.

The [financing of electoral campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_finance_in_the_United_States) in the United States happens at the federal, state, and local levels by contributions from individuals, corporations, and political action committees. According to the [Federal Election Commission](https://www.fec.gov/data/spending-bythenumbers/) (FEC) the total amount spent has been:

| Year | Total spending by all Senate candidates running that year |   |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------- | - |
| 2024 | \$1,687,323,291                                           |   |
| 2022 | \$1,708,197,866                                           |   |
| 2020 | £2,007,613,859                                            |   |

As at mid-August 2026, a total of \$666,336,000 (\$393,934,664 Democratic, \$261,005,865 Republican, and \$11,395,471 Other) has been spent by Senate candidates.

comments.author: nightsky81
comments.text:
I think the following context could be helpful for predicting this question.

1\) The authoritative source for resolving this question is the "Spending: by the numbers" figure reported on the FEC website, which sums disbursements by candidate campaign committees (which I will refer to as CCs). CCs are subject to [contribution limits](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/52/30116) but [receive favorable rates for campaign ads](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/47/315). The Background states: "The [financing of electoral campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_finance_in_the_United_States) in the United States happens at the federal, state, and local levels by contributions from individuals, corporations, and political action committees." For the sake of clarification, individuals and PACs, but not corporations, can contribute to CCs. Individuals and corporations can make unlimited contributions to [super PACs](https://www.fec.gov/press/resources-journalists/political-action-committees-pacs/), the primary component of [outside spending](https://www.opensecrets.org/outside-spending) in elections.

CC spending represents a little more than half of total election spending. The following table compares CC vs. outside spending over the previous 4 Senate election cycles.

| Year | CC (\$B) | Outside (\$B) | Total (\$B) | CCC % of Total |
| ---- | -------- | ------------- | ----------- | -------------- |
| 2018 | 1.056    | 0.647         | 1.703       | 62.0%          |
| 2020 | 2.008    | 1.517         | 3.525       | 57.0%          |
| 2022 | 1.708    | 1.313         | 3.021       | 56.5%          |
| 2024 | 1.687    | 1.380         | 3.067       | 55.0%          |

To reiterate, this question resolves to CC spending (as reported by the FEC, which I will discuss later) and not outside or total spending.

2\) The FEC mandates that CCs report their fundraising and spending according to a [predetermined schedule](https://www.fec.gov/help-candidates-and-committees/dates-and-deadlines/2026-reporting-dates/2026-quarterly-filers/). In theory, the Post-General and Year-End reporting periods, with deadlines of 12/03/2026 and 01/31/2027 respectively, lie after the scheduled resolution date of 12/02/2026. However, pursuant to Moderator DaAdCh's [clarification](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/45220/what-will-be-the-total-spending-by-senate-candidates-in-2026-us-election-cycle/#comment-1134116), I think it is reasonable to expect that Post-General reports will be counted, but not Year-End reports.

In [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Georgia_runoff_election) and [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_Senate_election_in_Georgia), Senate election runoffs in the state of Georgia resulted in a different filing schedule for the CCs involved in the runoff, which would have materially affected the resolution to this question for those years. Disregarding the effect of the 2022 runoff, the total Year-End reports for 2022 and 2024 totaled approximately \$20M in each year. This means that, for example, if this question had been asked regarding the 2024 Senate election cycle, I expect that the question would likely have resolved to \$1.667B instead of \$1.687B.

3\) I suspect some data quality issues with the FEC aggregation of the individual CC filings. In particular, according to Opus 5.5, the 2026 FEC headline figure of \$670,150,455.46 as of comment writing, as well as the 2024 FEC headline figure of \$1,687,323,291.13 contains, in addition to a slew of other issues and inconsistencies with little to no effect on the headline figure, the following major errors:

a) Double-counting: In 2024, Eric Hovde's CC was double counted because his CC was affiliated with two variants of his name (with and without his middle initial), and his CC's filings were added twice to the total. The effect of this error overstates the 2024 number by approximately \$32M.

b) Filings for John Barrasso (\~\$6.9M) and Barbara Lee (\~\$5.8M) in 2024 and for Raja Krishnamoorthi (\~\$31.5M) and Robin Kelly (\~\$3.5M) in 2026 were not included in the total. One possible root cause is that the metadata field of district\_number, which is relevant only for House candidates and should be recorded as 00 for Senate candidates, was None for all 4 candidates (as well as a number of other Senate candidates with negligible total spending). The effect of this error understates the 2024 number by approximately \$13M and the 2026 number by approximately \$35M.

Opus 5.5 did not find any errors of similar magnitude in the 2022 or 2020 FEC headline figure.

If true, these issues imply that the the authoritative source for resolving this question contains idiosyncratic errors which have little to do with campaign realities. I believe that, if real, these errors are unlikely to be fixed prior to question resolution, whether or not anyone attempts to alert the FEC (I did not attempt to reach out to the FEC).

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text:
The "most expensive Senate cycle ever" headlines are worth discounting here, because the resolution source doesn't count most of that money. The FEC dashboard only counts candidate committees, and AdImpact's \$3.4B projection is mostly super PAC and party money that never touches those totals. Looking at what does count: at the June 30 snapshot, Senate candidate disbursements were about \$711M in 2022 and \$682M in 2024, versus roughly \$670M this cycle per the live FEC API. Both prior cycles finished around 2.5x their June figure. So the candidate-side pace is running slightly behind, not ahead, even with Talarico and Ossoff burning tens of millions on ads. The June NRSC v. FEC ruling could push more spending through party committees rather than candidates, which would widen that gap.



Two things to watch: the October 15 Q3 filings (if Senate disbursements through September 30 come in above \~\$1.05B, the 2.5x pattern is holding), and whether the resolver waits for the December 3 post-general reports, which fall a day after this question closes. Without them, the dashboard would only reflect spending through mid-October and could be \$200–300M short of the eventual total.

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text:
@(DaAdCh) Quick clarification request, because it changes the whole mechanism of this question.

The FEC page only shows reports already filed. The chart below shows how much of each past cycle's final total was on the page on a given day. There's normally a big step on Dec 3, when the post-general reports (covering Oct 15 – Nov 23) come in.

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/Screenshot_2026-09-28_at_3.49.37PM.png)

So the resolution date decides which reports count:
\- Resolved on the Dec 2 page (as in the schedule resolution date): data through Oct 14 only.
\- Resolved on a later page as mentioned in the fine print(e.g., Dec 31): post-general reports included.

I am estimating a \~\$220M gap from timing alone, bigger than anything the actual campaigns will do. And it moves the right answer by roughly 20%.

Could you confirm which one counts?
